1.title: A Letter from a Prisoner
1.context: Paul had spent the better part of three years teaching in Ephesus (Acts 19), and later said farewell to its elders at Miletus, where they wept together (Acts 20:17–38). He now writes as a prisoner, and a letter is how his teaching still travels.
1.question: What do you notice about a blessing-filled letter that begins by naming its writer a prisoner?

1.title: Every Spiritual Blessing
1.context: In Paul’s Greek, verses 3–14 run as one long sentence of praise. The telling keeps that movement whole rather than breaking the blessing into separate points.
1.question: Which of the blessings named here (chosen, adopted, grace freely given) is hardest for you to believe is yours?

1.title: Redemption and the Mystery
1.context: Redemption was the language of buying someone out of slavery or debt. Mystery, in Paul’s use, is not a puzzle to solve but a plan of God once hidden and now announced openly.
1.question: What does it mean to you that forgiveness is described as riches lavished rather than measured out?

1.title: Chosen as God’s Own
1.context: Paul moves between “we” and “you” in this chapter. Here the “we” is the first who hoped in Christ; the next scene turns the same blessing toward the Ephesian readers themselves.
1.question: How does it land on you that God’s purpose for His people is their praise of His glory?

1.title: Sealed with the Spirit
1.context: A seal in the ancient world marked ownership and authenticity, like a signet pressed into wax. A pledge was a down payment, the first part of a sum that guaranteed the rest would follow.
1.question: Where in your life do you most need to remember that you are sealed and not left unclaimed?

2.title: He Has Not Stopped Praying
2.context: Paul cannot visit Ephesus, so the letter carries his prayers as well as his teaching. Reports of a church’s faith and love were how news traveled between the scattered believers.
2.question: Who prays for you by name, and who could you thank God for the way Paul does here?

2.title: The Eyes of Your Heart
2.context: Paul prays for sight rather than for changed circumstances. The hope of God’s calling and the riches of His inheritance are things he asks God to let them see.
2.question: If the eyes of your heart were opened wider, what do you think you would see first?

2.title: The Greatness of His Power
2.context: Paul measures God’s power toward believers by its greatest display he knows: raising Christ from the dead and seating Him at God’s right hand, an image of royal authority drawn from Psalm 110.
2.question: What situation in your life feels bigger than the power Paul describes here?

2.title: Head Over Everything
2.context: Rule, authority, power, and dominion were the ranked titles of unseen powers in the ancient world. Paul places every one of them beneath Christ, in this age and the age to come.
2.question: Which “name” in your world most competes for the place Paul gives to Christ here?

2.title: His Body, the Fullness
2.context: The letter’s first prayer ends not on the throne but on the church: the body of the One who fills all in all. This picture of the church will run through the whole letter.
2.question: What does it change in how you see your own church to hear it called Christ’s body and fullness?

3.title: Dead in Trespasses
3.context: Paul describes the old life in the language of walking, a picture of a whole way of life. He includes himself in the charge: “all of us” lived there, by nature children of wrath.
3.question: Which part of the old walk described here do you most recognize from your own past?

3.title: But God, Rich in Mercy
3.context: The sentence turns on two words, “But God.” In Paul’s telling the dead contribute nothing to being made alive; mercy and great love do the whole work.
3.question: Where have you seen God’s mercy reach someone who could do nothing to earn it?

3.title: Seated with Him
3.context: Paul speaks of believers as already raised and seated with Christ, and gives the reason as display: in the coming ages, God will show His grace by His kindness to them.
3.question: How does it affect your sense of the future to be called evidence of God’s grace?

3.title: By Grace Through Faith
3.context: This is among the most quoted sentences in the letter. Paul is careful with it: salvation is a gift, received by faith, so that boasting has no ground to stand on.
3.question: What is the difference, in your own experience, between receiving a gift and earning a wage?

3.title: God’s Workmanship
3.context: Workmanship carries the idea of something made by a craftsman. The good works in this verse come after the gift, prepared in advance like a road laid down before the walking starts.
3.question: What prepared work might be lying in front of you in this season of your life?

4.title: Remember What You Were
4.context: Paul now addresses the Gentile believers directly. Circumcision was the covenant sign of Israel; to be called “uncircumcised” was to be marked as an outsider to God’s people and His promises.
4.question: Why do you think Paul asks them to remember a past he also says is behind them?

4.title: Brought Near
4.context: Far and near are this chapter’s map of the world. The blood of Christ, not the effort of the far-off, is what closes the distance.
4.question: Who in your world is still “far away,” and what would being brought near look like for them?

4.title: He Himself Is Our Peace
4.context: Many readers connect the dividing wall with the barrier in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles at a distance on pain of death. Paul says Christ tore the wall down in His flesh and made one new humanity out of the two peoples.
4.question: Where do you see a dividing wall that peace has not yet reached?

4.title: Peace to the Far and the Near
4.context: The announcement of peace goes in both directions, to those who were far and those who were near. Access to the Father is the shared result, through Christ, by one Spirit.
4.question: What does it mean to you that both groups arrive by the same door?

4.title: Fellow Citizens, God’s Household
4.context: The picture changes from citizenship to architecture: a household, a building fitted together, a temple, with Christ as cornerstone, the stone that sets the lines for everything built on it.
4.question: In what ways are you being “built together” with other believers right now?

5.title: The Sentence That Stops
5.context: Paul begins a prayer at verse 1 and breaks off mid-sentence. He does not return to it until verse 14. The letter leaves the seam visible, and so does the telling.
5.question: What do you make of a prayer that waits thirteen verses to be finished?

5.title: The Stewardship of the Mystery
5.context: A steward managed a household on the owner’s behalf. Paul describes his knowledge of the mystery as something entrusted to him by revelation, to be read and understood by ordinary readers.
5.question: How does it strike you that this mystery is openly published rather than kept among a few?

5.title: Fellow Heirs
5.context: This single verse is the letter’s stated center: through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise.
5.question: Which of the three “fellow” words in this verse speaks most directly to you?

5.title: Less Than the Least
5.context: Paul’s self-description bends grammar to go lower: less than the least of all the saints. The riches he carries to the Gentiles he calls unsearchable, beyond tracing out.
5.question: How do you hold together Paul’s low view of himself and his high confidence in his message?

5.title: Boldness and Confidence
5.context: Paul says the church itself is the display through which God’s manifold wisdom is made known to rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms. His closing word in the scene is practical: do not be discouraged by his sufferings.
5.question: What helps you not lose heart when following Christ costs someone you love?

6.title: I Bow My Knees
6.context: The prayer resumes at the words where it broke off. Kneeling was less common than standing for prayer in Israel’s practice, and it signals earnestness. Every family derives its name from the one Father.
6.question: What does it mean to you that every family, in heaven and on earth, is named from one Father?

6.title: Strengthened in the Inner Being
6.context: The first request is for power, but inward: strengthened through the Spirit in the inner being, so that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, at home rather than visiting.
6.question: What would Christ being fully at home in your heart change about your ordinary days?

6.title: The Measure of Love
6.context: Paul measures love in four dimensions and then asks them to know a love that surpasses knowledge. The comprehension is communal: together with all the saints. These two paragraphs of the telling stand under one scene, as the prayer runs unbroken through them.
6.question: Who are the “all the saints” alongside whom you are learning the size of this love?

6.title: Immeasurably More
6.context: The doxology answers the prayer’s size with God’s: able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine. Glory is given to Him in the church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations.
6.question: What have you stopped asking for that this doxology might reopen?

7.title: Walk Worthy
7.context: At 4:1 the letter turns from what God has done to how His people walk. Walking was everyday language for a whole way of life. Unity here is something to preserve, not to invent.
7.question: Which of the manners named here (humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another) is your walk most short on?

7.title: Seven Ones
7.context: One body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Paul stacks the ones as the foundation under the church’s unity.
7.question: Which of the seven ones do you lean on most when believers around you disagree?

7.title: Gifts from the Ascended Christ
7.context: Paul quotes Psalm 68, a song of God ascending in victory, and reads its gifts as people given to the church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, given to equip the saints for ministry.
7.question: What gift has Christ given the church through people you know?

7.title: No Longer Infants
7.context: The goal of the gifts is maturity: the full measure of the stature of Christ. Its opposite is an infant in rough water, carried by every wind of teaching and every clever scheme.
7.question: Where do you feel yourself still tossed about, and what is helping you grow up?

7.title: The Whole Body Grows
7.context: Speaking the truth in love is the body’s growth habit. The head supplies, the ligaments hold, and each part’s work builds the whole up in love.
7.question: What is your part’s work in the body you belong to, as you understand it now?

8.title: No Longer Walk as the Gentiles Do
8.context: Paul describes the old walk from the inside: darkened understanding, hardness of heart, and a lost sense of shame. This Gentile walk is exactly what chapter 2 said his readers were rescued from.
8.question: Which step in the downward path described here do you most want to keep far from?

8.title: Put Off, Put On
8.context: The teaching uses the picture of clothing: an old self put off, a new self put on, created to be like God. The renewal of the mind stands between the two changes of clothes.
8.question: What is one piece of the old self you are still learning to leave off?

8.title: Truth, and the Anger Curfew
8.context: Members of one body cannot lie to one another without lying to themselves. Paul sets a psalm line inside his teaching, “Be angry, yet do not sin” (Psalm 4), and gives anger a sunset deadline.
8.question: Is there an anger in your life that has stayed past its sunset?

8.title: New Hands, New Speech
8.context: The thief’s hands are retrained for work and generosity. Speech is judged by what it builds. The warning about grieving the Holy Spirit recalls the seal of chapter 1: the sealed can still grieve the Sealer.
8.question: Whose building up could your next conversation be aimed at?

8.title: Forgiving as You Were Forgiven
8.context: Two lists face each other: bitterness, rage, anger, outcry, slander, malice on one side; kindness, tenderheartedness, and forgiveness on the other. The measure given is the forgiveness they themselves received in Christ.
8.question: Whom do you need to forgive at the measure Paul names here?

9.title: Imitators of God
9.context: Children imitate a father; that is the logic of the opening charge. The walk in love is measured by Christ’s self-giving, described in the language of sacrifice and a fragrant offering.
9.question: Whose imitation of God has most shaped your own walk?

9.title: Not Even a Hint
9.context: The standard is set at the level of a hint, and thanksgiving is put in the place of corrupt talk. Paul warns against empty words that talk people out of taking the warning seriously.
9.question: What fills your conversation where thanksgiving could stand instead?

9.title: Children of Light
9.context: The identity is stated before the behavior: you were darkness, now you are light in the Lord. The old saying Paul quotes, “Wake up, O sleeper,” is left as he leaves it, with no source named.
9.question: Where is light exposing something in your life, and what is it making visible?

9.title: Redeeming the Time
9.context: Redeeming the time pictures buying back something valuable in a market, in days Paul calls evil. Being filled with the Spirit shows itself in song, music in the heart, and thanks given for everything.
9.question: What would redeeming the time look like in your week as it actually stands?

9.title: Submit to One Another
9.context: This single verse is the hinge into the household teaching that follows. Mutual submission out of reverence for Christ is the sentence everything after it stands under.
9.question: What makes submitting to one another hard for you, and what makes it possible?

10.title: As Christ Loved the Church
10.context: The husband’s charge is framed by Christ’s self-giving: He loved the church and gave Himself up for her. The washing with water through the word pictures cleansing, and the goal is a church presented glorious and blameless.
10.question: How does the picture of Christ and the church shape your understanding of marriage, whether or not you are married?

10.title: Members of His Body
10.context: Paul quotes Genesis 2 on the two becoming one flesh, and then names his subject plainly: “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.” The summary returns the mystery to the household’s daily terms.
10.question: What does nourishing and cherishing look like in the closest relationship of your life?

10.title: The First Commandment with a Promise
10.context: Paul quotes the commandment from Exodus 20 and notes its attached promise of life going well. Fathers are charged not to provoke, but to bring children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
10.question: Who brought you up in the instruction of the Lord, and how are you passing it on?

10.title: One Master in Heaven
10.context: The letter addresses slaves and masters in the same household and puts both under one Master in heaven, with whom there is no favoritism. Masters are told to do the same for their slaves and to give up threats.
10.question: How does knowing there is no favoritism with God change the way you hold whatever authority you have?

11.title: Not Against Flesh and Blood
11.context: Finally is Paul’s own marker for the letter’s last movement. The struggle is named as spiritual, against rulers, authorities, and powers of this world’s darkness, not against flesh and blood.
11.question: How does this naming of the struggle change the way you face conflict with people?

11.title: Stand Firm
11.context: The armor’s pieces echo Isaiah’s pictures of God and His servant armed with righteousness and salvation. Standing, not advancing, is the verb Paul repeats: stand your ground, and having done everything, to stand.
11.question: Which piece of the first three (truth, righteousness, readiness of the gospel) feels thinnest on you today?

11.title: The Shield and the Sword
11.context: The shield of faith is the one piece Paul says to take up in addition to all the others; Roman soldiers’ large shields could be linked to cover a whole line. The sword of the Spirit, the word of God, is the armor’s one weapon.
11.question: What flaming arrows has faith already extinguished in your story?

11.title: An Ambassador in Chains
11.context: Prayer is carried as part of the armor passage itself. Paul’s request for himself is not release but boldness: an ambassador in chains asking to proclaim the mystery fearlessly, as he should.
11.question: If you asked for prayer the way Paul does here, what would you ask for?

11.title: Grace to All Who Love Him
11.context: Tychicus, called a beloved brother and faithful servant, is sent so the church may know how Paul is and be encouraged. The letter closes with peace, love with faith, and grace to all who love the Lord Jesus with an undying love.
11.question: Who has been a Tychicus to you, carrying news and encouragement at the right time?
